title: Polymers and Chemistry in Everyday Life
subcategory: Polymers / Chemistry in Everyday Life — Classification, Drugs, Everyday Chemicals

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part II, Class 12 — Polymers; Chemistry in Everyday Life

summary: Polymers form either by simple addition of identical monomer units (retaining all atoms) or by condensation with loss of a small molecule at each linkage step; everyday chemistry classifies drugs by their target biological receptor/effect and distinguishes closely related terms like antiseptics from disinfectants by where they can safely be applied.
explanation: ADDITION polymers form when unsaturated monomer units (containing a C=C double bond) simply add to one another repeatedly (typically via a free-radical, cationic, or anionic chain mechanism) with NO small molecule lost — the polymer's molecular formula is exactly an integer multiple of the monomer's (e.g. polythene from ethylene, PVC from vinyl chloride). CONDENSATION polymers form when monomer units (usually bearing two reactive functional groups, e.g. a diol + a diacid, or a diamine + a diacid) join with the repeated LOSS of a small molecule (commonly water) at each new linkage — e.g. nylon-6,6 (from hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid, losing water at each amide linkage) and terylene/PET (from ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid, losing water at each ester linkage). Polymers are also classified by their response to heat: THERMOPLASTIC polymers (linear or slightly branched chains, e.g. polythene, PVC) soften on heating and can be remoulded repeatedly; THERMOSETTING polymers (heavily cross-linked, e.g. bakelite) undergo a permanent, irreversible chemical change on initial heating/moulding and cannot be remelted afterward. Biodegradable polymers (like PHBV) are specifically designed with linkages (often ester-based) that microorganisms can break down naturally, unlike most conventional synthetic polymers which persist in the environment for a very long time. In everyday/medicinal chemistry: ANALGESICS relieve pain (narcotic analgesics like morphine act on the central nervous system/opioid receptors and can be habit-forming; non-narcotic analgesics like aspirin and paracetamol do not act on the CNS this way and are not habit-forming); ANTIPYRETICS reduce fever; ANTISEPTICS are chemicals applied to LIVING tissue (skin, wounds) to kill/prevent growth of microorganisms (e.g. dilute iodine tincture, hydrogen peroxide at low concentration); DISINFECTANTS are similar chemicals but too harsh for living tissue and are applied only to INANIMATE objects/surfaces (e.g. 1% phenol solution used on floors — notably, the SAME chemical, like phenol, can act as either an antiseptic or a disinfectant purely depending on its CONCENTRATION). Artificial sweeteners (e.g. aspartame, saccharin) provide sweetness without the caloric content of natural sugars, useful for diabetics/calorie-conscious diets; soaps (sodium/potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids) clean via micelle formation but are ineffective in hard water (form insoluble scum with Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺), which is one key reason synthetic detergents were developed.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming all polymers form by the same (addition) mechanism — condensation polymers form through a fundamentally different pathway (stepwise linkage with loss of a small molecule like water at each step), and their empirical formula is NOT simply a multiple of one single monomer.

Using 'antiseptic' and 'disinfectant' as fully interchangeable terms — the key distinction is WHERE they can safely be applied (living tissue vs inanimate surfaces), and notably the exact same chemical (like phenol) can be either, depending purely on concentration.
Believing all analgesics are habit-forming/addictive — this applies specifically to NARCOTIC analgesics (opioids); non-narcotic analgesics like paracetamol and aspirin are not addictive in this way.
examples: Nylon-6,6 is a condensation polymer formed from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, with water released at each new amide bond formed.
Dilute (0.2%) phenol solution acts as an antiseptic on skin, while a more concentrated (1%) phenol solution is used as a disinfectant on floors and instruments, not on living tissue.
genZNote: Condensation polymers: can't form a bond without kicking out a water molecule every single time.
